title: AI is killing All About Berlin
titleZh: AI is killing All About Berlin
author: grey-area
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Posted on May 26, 2026 Psst! There is an update to this post.

This is the traffic to All About Berlin, the website that I run since 2017, and live from since 2020. After 7 years of growth, it has lost 70% 75% of its traffic to Google AI Overviews. When you Googled something, you used to get a link to my website. Now you get a page of ads, then an AI-generated answer trained on my content, then finally a link to my website. This has a devastating impact on traffic. What it means to be first on Google It’s hard to fund my work with only a quarter of my audience. Soon, I will need another way to pay my rent. Instead of writing new guides, I already spend my days preparing for that future. It’s not just about the money. I have poured 8 years of my life into making something good and useful. Strangers’ faces light up when they learn that I run All About Berlin. Local and federal government offices refer people to my guides. The Berlin immigration office uses my data about themselves. It inspired two government portals and a few similar websites in other cities. If my work just get mixed into an AI-generated answer, I lose my voice and my audience. My carefully chosen words lose their meaning. No one shakes my hand and buys me a beer. No one tells me how their citizenship application went. This is not an isolated case. Many website owners have reached out in private to commiserate. Some have paywalled their work. Others have given up and moved on. They keep the websites online, but they no longer update them. It’s just not worth it. It will get worse. Last week, Google has made two announcements: AI-generated answers will replace search results entirely, and they have ads in them.1 This is the future of the internet. No websites, just a chat box with ads. I don’t know where All About Berlin fits in that future.
This was also discussed on Mastodon, Hacker News, LinkedIn and Twitter. If you are affected, reach out. Let me know how you are doing. You are not going through this alone.

Big discussion on Hacker News The Telegraph Forbes The Indicator by NPR Deutschlandfunk The Ringer OMR PPC Land Handpicked Berlin NDTV Stockhouse Clarin Press.pl H7O magazine Root.cz Adevarul Pineberry

comments.author: jeppester
comments.textRawHtml:
How do you all feel about the situation?

Is it just okay that these humongous companies just took all our work without paying us a dime?

Is it okay that they are replacing our jobs with tech that would never have existed had they not taken all that work? (or would have moved slower)

Do you feel good supporting these companies by giving them money every month?

What do you think will happen if these companies become profitable? Do you think it will have a positive effect on our society?

Personally I feel that I'm living with severe chronic cognitive dissonance - and have been for many months at this point. But I'm not sure what I can do, I have rent to pay and children to feed.

Do you all just not have this feeling? How do you combat it?

children.author: shinycode
children.textRawHtml:
I have a deep feeling that it’ll never be for our good. The strategy is “get them addicted first”, then “remove human thinking and understanding” (junior don’t learn like we did in 2000-2010) then they’ll do whatever they want. They will provide the cloud and the code and the voice for anything software related, eating up everything that is in the middle.

We can’t escape it. They are too powerful and because there is positive side effects as well, and they know it, there will always be a debate.

I feel that, the common mindset in software that you rarely see elsewhere, like in big pharma, is to open and give knowledge very broadly. But OpenAI, Anthropic absorbed everything and are not playing along. They should have continued giving free knowledge of everything as well. That’s only fair, but that’s just one way to see it.

children.author: boringg
children.textRawHtml:
Its the forever problem of AI - its like a one time reaping of high quality data and then information goes stale because few people will provide information for free, fewer people will be motivated to build any content online, most things will get protected and locked down, open source is saturated with agents.

This is 100% the "glory" days of AI. The price is highly subsidized by investors, govt but thats going to ramp up and the product quality will dilute as they need to drive revenue for the markets. Its the same long lived strategy of every great tech company that has VC returns to feed. If OpenAI can stay private for a longer period of time they could ostensibly continue to build a better product and not be handcuffed to wallstreet in the near term.

Cost of AI will get subsidized for 3-4 years while corporate america gets addicted, then pricing will ramp up and corporate ameria will be dependent. This has been said millions of times over.

children.author: ryandrake
children.textRawHtml:
I think using AI in 10 years will feel like using StackOverflow today. SO is kind of stuck in time, where every answer there is how you’d do things in 2015. They structurally can’t seem to let go of old answers and ingest new information, so they are dying in the past.

The same might happen to AI if it stops having access to fresh information. If people move to walled gardens that can’t be consumed by AI then there is a chance that these products eventually get stuck in the past, too. I don’t know what would be a walled enough garden for this, but it might happen.

children.author: fakedang
children.textRawHtml:
I see two distinct possibilities:

1.) The web and software code get stuck in the past, as everything gets built with outdated styles, a leftover from the open source era.

2.) A few companies that can, like Vercel, will build new UI or new APIs and backend structures and gate access to them with their own proprietary models. They will make their docs internal or not readable by AI bots, like what Tailwind did.

children.author: redwood
children.textRawHtml:
The same was said about Uber and Lyft in other words that once Venture Capital subsidies ended the prices would be passed on to consumers. While it's true on inflation adjusted basis is not that extreme from its low point maybe 30% higher.

And with Rideshare you have a fundamental cost of a car and a person whereas with AI costs can quickly be reduced across multiple dimensions of optimizations Hardware stack architecture region energy costs latency and other trade-offs. Then you have open models competing to bring costs down. So I just don't know that we'll ever see the cost go up

children.author: asdff
children.textRawHtml:
Rideshare is interesting because uber et al might actually be cheaper per ride than waymo et al. Yes, they pay a driver a very low wage which is some overhead, but they don't own any cars. The driver pays for the car, its maintenance, registration and insurance, fueling, and storage. It is dubious if it even pencils out for anyone but the power users in the gig economy. Waymo has massive overhead with its fleet requirements, on the other hand, real estate requirements as well.

AI could be similar. The costs of the bleeding edge are probably enormous. But imagine if your competitor was some cheap model, with a layer of southeast asians between the user and the model getting the apparent quality of the model far higher leveraging some cheap expert human prompters. There's some odds there that they might route you at the bleeding edge. Plus also, plenty of users probably aren't even that sensitive to a low quality vs high quality response for their purposes.

children.author: toonvanvr
children.textRawHtml:
I think that value moved and we're feeling this pain because we're chasing ghosts: working on the after-image of where value used to be is a lost cause and we all feel it in fear of our own jobs.

In my expectation, governments who embrace AI and regulate on misuse rather than on protecting old structures will unlock access to the new value chains earlier on and get first-mover advantage. I hope Europe sees this instead of regulating us into pre-AI protectioninsm in an AI world.

There are so many opportunities to make the world better in line with the right-to-repair movement and their open data incentives. They were on the right track, I just hope they don't fall for the old money corruption, because that will cost way more to lower class people along the way than AI on its own ever would.

I think you yourself are an example of this. The ideas that all regulation is harmful and that plucky upstart tech firms will save us were overly optimistic years ago, and now we know they aren't correct.

The danger is not old money corruption and protectionism; it's the new money robber barons of the tech industry.

children.author: majormajor
children.textRawHtml:
AI and old-money protectionism are likely going exactly the same place: access to more things for old-money, reduced opportunities to carve out new things for those without. Just copy the new faster and cheaper than ever. Embrace-extend-extinguish at a class-level.

So many of the things that can be automated away don't really have higher-level value chains to move to. The value was other people reducing friction for you or presenting you with novelty. The AI-maximalist/old-money goals here are identical: avoid having to pay a person for that.

The core underlying assumption in both POVs—whether "shape rotators" or "old money elites"—is that everything boils down to manipulating abstractions. The world, to these groups, isn't about people living satisfying individual lives. It's about making things as convenient for themselves as possible, not about doing concrete things in the real world for people as a whole. They are (intentionally) replacing the territory with the map.

children.author: hdndjsbbs
children.textRawHtml:
There was a funny neoliberal concept in the late 20th century that everyone was going to transition to an information economy. That China and Brazil and Sub-Saharan Africa were just behind the curve, and if they learned to code they could also have an American standard of living.

It's obviously bullshit, because the American standard of living is based on extraction and exploitation elsewhere. If you make everyone rich, there's no gradient to exploit. If everyone everywhere does office jobs, who will work in the mines?

The AI trend is the pigeons coming home to roost. Oligarchs have extracted value from overseas, but now they also need to extract value from the underclass at home more aggressively than ever. The number has to go up.

children.author: ost-ing
children.textRawHtml:
I actually think the only way to stop society collapsing is to have very strong AI safeguards and labor regulations. Its simply too powerful and disruptive to be allowed to run wild.

AI doesn't have to replace people, and it doesn't have to dumb us down. We need to do some economic re-modelling, otherwise capitalism will crumble and society will with it. I just don't see any other way, but I'm also terrified we will enter some dystopian Sam Altman Worldcoin reality where everyone has to scan their iris' to cryptographically sign anything uploaded onto the internet.

Either way, we have to get the balance right which will be very difficult... The alternative is terrifying.
